original_title: I Hope GTA 6 Borrows a Lot From GTA 4

en.title: GTA 6 Should Channel GTA 4's Gritty Soul, Not Just Its Shine
en.summary: As anticipation for Grand Theft Auto 6 reaches a fever pitch, one veteran journalist argues that the upcoming title should look back to GTA 4's strengths. It's a call for depth over sheer spectacle.
en.body:
The roar of anticipation for **Grand Theft Auto 6** is deafening, and with every passing day, speculation intensifies about what Rockstar Games has in store. While the sheer ambition and scale of **GTA 5** are undeniable, a recent re-immersion into **Grand Theft Auto 4** has sparked a compelling argument: perhaps the future of Liberty City's successor lies in embracing the past. It’s not about replicating the past, but about channeling its unique spirit.

**GTA 4**’s Liberty City, despite its technical limitations compared to today's standards, offered a *lived-in* grittiness that many feel has been somewhat lost in the series’ evolution. The original Xbox 360 version’s poor draw distance, while a stark reminder of technological progress, couldn’t obscure the meticulous effort Rockstar poured into world-building. The atmosphere was palpable, a grimy, realistic portrayal of the American dream's underbelly. Niko Bellic remains one of gaming’s most compelling protagonists, a complex figure whose narrative arc felt deeply personal and grounded, a far cry from the more caricatured personalities of **GTA 5**.

## The Enduring Appeal of Niko's Story

While **Grand Theft Auto 5** might be a personal favorite for its blockbuster scope and mission design, **GTA 4** arguably tells the best story in the franchise’s history. Niko Bellic’s journey, fraught with moral ambiguity and the harsh realities of immigrant life in America, resonated with players on a profound level. His struggles felt genuine, making him a more complete rendering of the human experience than the often exaggerated antics of Michael, Franklin, and Trevor. This focus on character depth and a more mature, nuanced narrative is precisely what many fans hope **GTA 6** will recapture, moving beyond pure spectacle to deliver an emotionally resonant experience.

## What Fans Are Saying

The sentiment is clear among many long-time players: **GTA 6** has a massive opportunity to blend the unparalleled technical prowess and expansive open-world design we expect from Rockstar with the narrative depth and character-driven storytelling that made **GTA 4** so unforgettable. The 13-year gap between **GTA 5** and **GTA 6** suggests a leap in technology akin to a propeller plane versus a fighter jet, but the true innovation will come from how Rockstar uses that power to tell a story that matters. The decision to withhold early review copies from journalists and influencers, a move aimed at preventing plot leaks, also underscores Rockstar's awareness of how crucial the narrative is to the **GTA 6** experience.

## What's Next

Rockstar Games has not yet announced a release date for **Grand Theft Auto 6**, but the game is widely anticipated to launch in 2025 or 2026, with details on its specific platform availability to follow. Fans are eagerly awaiting any official word on when they can expect to step back into the world of Grand Theft Auto.

content_raw: Maybe it’s the excitement of knowing we’re about to see a whole load of GTA 6 soon, or maybe it was just another weekend where it felt too hot to move, but I decided to boot up Grand Theft Auto 4 for the first time in 18 years. This may not surprise many of you, but I’m here to tell you that it’s still very fun. Niko still rules. I love the lived-in feel of Liberty City. I even really enjoy the driving — somewhat controversial, I know. What I’m trying to say is: GTA 4 is still good, innit. IGN gave GTA 4 a 10 way back in the day (I didn’t review it; I was still in school at the time), and, while I may not agree with it being a full-fledged masterpiece, there’s still plenty to admire. I’m not going to give it a full re-appraisal here; that’s what my colleague Luke Reilly will be doing when he gets round to it on our GTA legacy review series . I’m just here to let you know it still has the juice. I won’t lie, though, the first thing I noticed when booting GTA 4 up was a sign of just how far we’ve come since Rockstar’s first hi-def city. The draw distance is really poor, at least on the original Xbox 360 version. Really, it was as if someone had stolen my glasses, proceeded to rub mud into my eyes, and then asked me to look directly into the sun. When things do come into focus, though, it becomes clear just how much effort Rockstar put into this version of Liberty City’s character. Technical limitations didn’t prevent some first-class world-building here, especially the really grimy atmosphere that coats the opening areas of this New York proxy. Niko’s first apartment is suitably cramped for the start of this American dream story — the tape barely holding the lad's mag posters to the wall, each bikini model sporting more fold lines than tan lines. It’s a classy(?) touch. There’s no denying that you feel far more in control of a car in GTA 5, but I miss the danger of its predecessor’s driving. The slapdash feeling continues when you step outside and into Roman’s taxi, with its rear bumper clinging on for dear life as you push the accelerator. The handling of vehicles in GTA 4 has been a topic of heated conversation since it first came out, but I have to admit, I kinda like it. There’s a looseness in how you corner that adds unexpected thrills to chases. Yes, it does make some roads feel like ice has been layered over the top of the asphalt, a feeling only enhanced by cars that feel heavy to the point of wondering if someone has lumped a pallet of bricks in the trunk as a prank, but I’d be lying if I said I didn’t prefer it to what would come five years later. There’s no denying that you feel far more in control of a car in GTA 5, but I miss the danger of its predecessor’s driving. I’d love GTA 6 to find a balance between the two.
